title: Meta-Learning for Compositionality
subtitle: An intuitive walk through Lake and Baroni's Nature paper on how a plain neural network can learn to combine known parts in new ways
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: An intuitive, step-by-step retelling of the open-access Nature paper Human-like systematic generalization through a meta-learning neural network by Brenden Lake and Marco Baroni (Nature 623, 115-121, 2023, CC BY 4.0). Learn what systematic generalization is, play a made-up colour language, meet the three human habits the paper measures, see why ordinary networks stumble, and follow the meta-learning for compositionality (MLC) recipe, its results and its limits, with numbered figures, recaps, memory tricks, concept maps and short Python labs. The examples and words in this course are our own illustrations in the spirit of the paper, and this course is not affiliated with or endorsed by the authors or the journal.

summary: People understand new combinations of words they already know. If you know what skip means and what twice means, you understand skip twice the first time you hear it. This skill is called systematic generalization, or compositionality.

In 1988 the scientists Jerry Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn argued that neural networks could not do this. For decades the argument has been debated, and even today's big networks often stumble on tests of it.

In 2023 Brenden Lake and Marco Baroni published a paper in the journal Nature that trains a plain neural network in a new way, called meta-learning for compositionality or MLC. This course walks through that paper step by step.

items: ELI5. You know what jump means and you know what twice means. Someone says jump twice for the very first time and you just do it. You never needed a lesson for that exact phrase, because you snap the pieces together like Lego.

Now the real words. Snapping known parts together in new ways is called systematic generalization, or compositionality. In 1988 two scientists said computer brains could not do it. This course follows a 2023 paper that shows a way for a plain neural network to do it.
Try it. Pick three action words and three modifiers, such as twice and backwards, and count how many phrases you can build. Then notice how few you would need to hear to understand them all.
If you remember one thing: known parts, new combinations.

Think about learning a new word. Suppose you learn the word skip. Then someone says skip backwards. You have never heard those two together, yet you know exactly what to do. You did not need a lesson for that sentence.
That everyday magic is called systematic generalization. You take parts you already know and snap them together in a new way. Language works like Lego: a few pieces, endlessly many buildings.

The grid in the figure shows the idea. The green boxes are phrases you have met. The dashed pink boxes are phrases you have never met. A person who understands the pieces can read every box. (See Figure 1.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 1.1. Known parts in new combinations. Green boxes were seen, dashed boxes were not.

items: Why is this a big deal for computers? In 1988, Jerry Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn wrote that neural networks could not do this kind of thing, because a network just matches patterns it has seen. They said real thinking needs rules for combining parts.

Many experiments since then agree that ordinary neural networks struggle. They can learn the phrases in their training set, but they often fail on new combinations. Even recent giant language models still make systematic mistakes on carefully built tests, as the paper's supplement reports for GPT-4.

This is the puzzle the paper tackles. Can a plain neural network, with no hand-built rule machinery, become systematic like people? The authors say yes, if it is trained in the right way. The rest of this course unpacks how.

summary: To study systematic generalization, the researchers invented a small made-up language. A handful of nonsense words stand for coloured circles, and a few function words act on them.
Each sentence has an exact answer, a row of coloured circles, that you can work out by following rules. The rules are called an interpretation grammar.
The words and rules in this course are our own simple illustration in the same spirit as the paper's task. The meanings of the words are different for every person, so nobody can have memorised them.

ELI5. Imagine a secret game language. A few silly words name coloured circles and a few helper words say what to do with them: repeat three times, sandwich, or swap places. Once you know the little rules, any sentence has exactly one right answer.

Now the real words. The words that name things are primitives. The helper words are function words. The rules that give every sentence its answer are the interpretation grammar. The paper's meanings are shuffled for every person so nobody can cheat by remembering.
Try it. Work out lug fep kiki wif: lug fep is three blue circles, wif is one green, and kiki puts the green part first. Then check yourself in the interpreter lab.
If you remember one thing: colours, helper words, and a recipe that gives one right answer.
Imagine a game with a secret language. There are four colour words: dax is red, wif is green, lug is blue and zup is yellow. When you say a colour word, you point at a circle of that colour.

Words like these, that name one thing directly, are called primitives. Now add words that do things to other words. We call them function words, just like a function in a program takes input and returns an output.

Our first function word is fep. It repeats the circle three times: dax fep means red red red. The second is blicket. It sandwiches: wif blicket dax means green, red, green. The third is kiki. It swaps the order: lug kiki wif means green, blue.
The figure below lists all of them. Notice how little there is to learn: seven words in total. Yet they combine into endless sentences. (See Figure 2.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 2.1. Our tiny pseudolanguage: four colour words and three function words.

items: Sentences are read in pieces. In lug fep kiki wif the word kiki splits the sentence into two parts. The left part, lug fep, makes three blue circles. The right part, wif, is one green circle. Kiki then puts the right part first, so you get green then three blue. (See Figure 2.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 2.2. Reading lug fep kiki wif in pieces.

lesson.code:
# a tiny interpreter for our language
lex = {'dax': 'R', 'wif': 'G', 'lug': 'B', 'zup': 'Y'}
print(lex['lug'] * 3)  # lug fep
print('G' + 'R' + 'G')   # wif blicket dax
print('G' + 'B')        # lug kiki wif

items: The rules for combining pieces are called an interpretation grammar. A grammar is a recipe that says how the meaning of a whole sentence comes from its parts. Our recipe is: split on kiki, then split each part on blicket, then apply fep to repeat.

In the paper's experiment the word meanings are changed for every participant, so dax might be red for you and blue for someone else. That is the key. Nobody can rely on memory of the language, and everybody must figure the rules out from the examples they get.

The paper's own task uses the same kind of design: four primitive words that map to coloured circles and three function words. Ours is simplified and not a copy of their stimuli, but the thinking skills needed are the same.
Memory trick: Fep Fills, Blicket Bread, Kiki Kicks. Fep Fills three copies, Blicket makes a sandwich (bread, filling, bread), Kiki Kicks the order around.

summary: In the paper's first experiment, 25 people learned such a language from only 14 study examples and then answered 10 new questions. This is few-shot learning: very few examples.
People matched the exact rule 80.7 percent of the time, and 72.5 percent of their answers were right even when the answer was longer than any study example. Their mistakes were not random.
The mistakes followed habits that you will meet in the next chapter. These habits are the clue that the researchers wanted their network to copy.

ELI5. Picture a classroom game. You get fourteen clues about a made-up language, then ten new puzzles. Most grown-ups get most puzzles right, and when they slip, they slip in the same few ways.

Now the real words. This is the few-shot experiment: 14 study examples and 10 queries for each of 25 people. People matched the exact rule 80.7 percent of the time and were right 72.5 percent of the time on answers longer than any they studied.
Try it. Play the alien language lab. You get a fresh language each time. Count how many you get right and see whether your slips look like the people in the study.
If you remember one thing: people are good at this, but not perfect, and their slips have patterns.

Here is how the first experiment went. A person sat down and saw a few instructions with their answers, such as a word and its coloured circle. They studied 14 of these. The study moved in four stages from single words to words with functions.

Then came the test. The person saw 10 new instructions with no answers and had to build each answer from coloured circles. Some queries were chosen so that the answer was longer than any answer in the study set. That is a harder test of the rules.

The figure shows the results. In 80.7 percent of the 10-query answers, people produced exactly the answer the rules give. On the harder long-answer queries they were right 72.5 percent of the time. For people who see a made-up language for a few minutes, that is a strong performance.
(See Figure 3.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 3.1. The few-shot experiment: study 14, answer 10, and the two headline results.

items: The researchers recruited 30 people online and excluded 5 who missed the easy catch trials, leaving 25. Every person got a different assignment of words to meanings, so nobody could share answers or rely on a pattern from the internet.

Now the interesting part. When people were wrong, they were not wrong at random. About a quarter of the errors followed one pattern: using one circle per word, as if each word made its own piece. Another common mistake was to just write the pieces in the order they appeared.
These patterns hint at hidden habits.

Habits like these are important for the research question. The paper wants a neural network that is as systematic as people and also as human-like in its mistakes. A perfect rule follower would be too clean. People are somewhere between clean rules and flexible guesses.
Try it yourself in the lab below. You will get a fresh language each time. Study the examples, then answer the questions. You may find that you make the same kind of slips as the people in the study.

summary: When examples do not settle an answer, people lean on built-in habits called inductive biases. The paper finds three that matter in this task: one-to-one mapping, iconic concatenation and mutual exclusivity.
In a second experiment, 29 people guessed answers to seven instructions with no examples at all. That reveals their habits in the open. Most people used all of the habits at once.
The goal of the paper is a network that is systematic like an algebra and also has these human habits, without having them written in by hand.

ELI5. When you do not know an answer, your mind has habits to fall back on, like a favourite default. You tend to give each word its own piece, keep the pieces in the order you heard, and never give two different questions the same answer.

Now the real words. These defaults are called inductive biases. The three in the paper are one-to-one mapping, iconic concatenation and mutual exclusivity. In the open-ended test 93.1 percent of people gave every instruction its own unique answer, and 58.6 percent used all three habits together.

Try it. Make up an instruction with a word you have never seen and guess its colours. Notice that you probably listed the colours of the known words, in order, and wanted your answers to differ from one another.
If you remember one thing: one piece per word, order kept, different words give different answers.

Suppose someone shows you the words dax and wif with their colours and then asks what dax zorp wif means. You never saw zorp. What do you write? Most people write red then green: the pieces for the words they know, in the order they appear.

That is a habit. When knowledge runs out, the mind falls back on a default guess. Scientists call such a default an inductive bias: a push in a certain direction that comes from inside the learner, not from the examples.

The paper highlights three such habits. The first is one-to-one mapping. A word gets its own piece of the answer: two known words give two circles. The second is iconic concatenation: the pieces come in the same order as the words. (See Figure 4.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.1. The three habits: one-to-one, iconic order, mutual exclusivity.

items: The third is mutual exclusivity. If two different instructions both appear, give them different answers. People assume that different words mean different things. Children use the same trick when they learn language.
The researchers measured this in a second experiment. In it, 29 people saw no examples at all and simply guessed answers to seven instructions. Doing this with no help shows the habits in the open.

The figure shows the result. A strong 93.1 percent gave each instruction its own unique answer. 79.3 percent used iconic concatenation, 62.1 percent used one-to-one mappings, and 58.6 percent used all three together. (See Figure 4.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.2. How many people used each habit in the open-ended task.

items: Why does this matter for machines? A plain neural network trained the usual way has no reason to prefer these guesses. A perfect symbolic program would follow the exact rule but would have no flexible guessing at all. People sit between. The researchers wanted a network that sits there too.

There is a neat twist. The habits are not wired into the network. They are written into the examples the network practises on, as you will see when we meet the training recipe. The network learns the habits from data, the way a child might.
Memory trick: OOO: One, Order, Other. One piece per word, Order kept, Other words get other answers.

summary: A standard neural network learns from many examples of one fixed task. It can memorise the training phrases very well, but memorising is not understanding.
In the paper, a basic sequence-to-sequence network with no study examples and no meta-learning scored zero percent exact match on the few-shot task, because it never sees the new meanings.
The network MLC uses is just as ordinary: a transformer with an encoder and a decoder. The difference is what it has been trained to do, not how it is built.

ELI5. Think of a student who learns every answer in the textbook by heart. Ask a question from the book and the answer is perfect. Change one name in the question and the student is lost, because they never learned the idea, only the answers.

Now the real words. A standard network trained on a fixed task is a memoriser. It scored zero percent on the few-shot task because the word meanings had changed. The network in the paper is an ordinary transformer: an encoder reads the input and a decoder writes the answer symbol by symbol.
Try it. Run the memoriser lab: it answers only questions it has seen and prints a question mark for everything else. That is exactly what we do not want from a learner.
If you remember one thing: memorising is not understanding.

What happens when you train a normal network on our language? Give it thousands of sentences and answers. It will learn them. But if the meaning of dax changes for the next person, everything it memorised is wrong.

A good learner should not need to retrain for each new language. It should read the examples it is given and work out the meanings on the spot, like a person. A normal network has no way to do that, because its examples live in its training, not in its input.

The paper's baseline, a basic sequence-to-sequence network, shows this. It gets no study examples at test time. Its exact-match accuracy on the few-shot task is zero. It is a pure memoriser trying to guess at meanings it never saw.

Now meet the machine they use. It is a transformer. You can think of it as two parts. The encoder reads everything in the input and builds a rich description of it. The decoder then writes the answer one symbol at a time, glancing back at the encoder's description.

The figure shows the setup. In MLC the input is a single long string. It holds the study examples and the query together. So at test time the network has the examples in front of it, just like a person does. (See Figure 5.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 5.1. The encoder-decoder transformer that reads study examples and the query together.

items: This network is small: 3 layers and about 1.4 million adjustable numbers. By today's standards that is tiny. There are no special rule engines inside. The authors want to show that the training procedure, not clever hardware, makes the difference.

The code above is the memoriser in miniature. It answers questions it has seen and says a question mark for everything else, even lug on its own. A systematic learner would work out that lug means blue from lug fep. That reasoning step is what we want from a neural network.

summary: Meta-learning means practising the skill of learning itself. Instead of learning one task, a network sees a long stream of small tasks, each with its own examples.
Because the meanings of the words change in every task, the network cannot memorise them. The only thing that helps across tasks is the skill of reading the examples and working out the rule.
That skill is what we want: look at a few examples, work out the pattern, apply it to a new question.

ELI5. Imagine learning a new board game every day, with new rules each time. You stop memorising rules and start getting really good at working them out from a few turns. That is learning how to learn.

Now the real words. This is meta-learning. Each small game is an episode with a few study examples and a query. The word meanings change in every episode, so the network can only succeed by reading the examples. At test time its weights are frozen and the new language is just part of its input.

Try it. Open the episode lab and press Next episode a few times. Each time dax means something different. Then press Solve it to watch a rule finder rule out impossible meanings, one example at a time.
If you remember one thing: practise on a stream of changing tasks and you learn to learn.

When you were small, you did not learn each new game from scratch. You got good at learning games: watch a few turns, spot the rule, play. That skill, learning to learn, is what meta-learning tries to train.

To train it, you do not show one big task. You show many small ones. Each small task is called an episode. An episode has a few study examples and one query, a question to answer using those examples.

The figure compares the two ways of training. On the left is the usual way: one fixed world, the same answers again and again. On the right is a stream of episodes in which dax means red in one, green in another, blue in a third. (See Figure 6.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 6.1. Standard training sees one world. Meta-training sees a new world each episode.

items: In the stream, the meaning of every word is shuffled. So the network can never rely on remembering what dax means. The only thing that works in every episode is reading the study examples and working out the meanings fresh.

After lots of practice the network has not learned the meaning of any word. It has learned something deeper: a procedure for finding meanings from examples and combining them. That procedure is the thing that generalises to a new language, just like people.

Here is the crucial point about how this is used afterwards. At test time the network's weights are frozen. No learning happens in the usual sense. The new task is handled by feeding the study examples in as part of the input. The network does the rest in a single forward pass.

summary: MLC stands for meta-learning for compositionality. It is a recipe for training a standard transformer on a stream of episodes made from randomly generated grammars.

Each episode has study examples and a query. The target answer is the exact rule answer 80 percent of the time and a human-like guess 20 percent of the time, so the network learns both rules and habits.
Because the guessing habits are written into the targets, the network learns them from data. The network itself has no built-in rules.

ELI5. A cook invents a thousand made-up cuisines, each with new names for the same ingredients, and practises cooking from a few tasting spoons each time. Most dishes follow the rules, but a few follow human tastes instead.

Now the real words. The MLC recipe draws a random grammar for each episode, packs study examples and a query into one input, and sets the target to the exact rule answer 80 percent of the time and a human-like guess 20 percent of the time. The network is a plain transformer.
Try it. Use the Pack the input lab to build the one-string input for an episode, then the Pick the target lab to practise the 80 and 20 split.
If you remember one thing: random grammars, many episodes, mixed targets, a plain network.

Now we can put the pieces together. To build one episode, the recipe first draws a brand-new grammar at random: a new set of word meanings and function rules. It then writes study examples and a query using that grammar.

All of it goes into the network as one string, with the study examples and then the query. The network must output the answer for the query. The figure shows an episode. You can see the study examples, the query and the target. (See Figure 7.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 7.1. Anatomy of one training episode and how its target is chosen.

items: How is the target chosen? Here is the clever bit. In 80 percent of episodes, the target is the strict algebraic answer: exactly what the rules say. In the other 20 percent, it is a human-like answer that follows the habits from the last chapter.

The 80 and 20 are tuned so that the network's overall accuracy is similar to people's. Because the habits only show up in the targets, nothing special is added to the network. It simply learns from data that sometimes answers follow rules and sometimes follow human guessing habits.

The paper trains several versions. In MLC the targets are exact algebraic answers and bias-based answers. In algebraic-only MLC the targets are strictly the rules. In joint MLC the network is trained on both the few-shot task and the open-ended task, with extra bridging episodes.
The copy-only version practises just copying study examples.

lesson.code:
# build the one-string input the network reads
study = [['dax', 'R'], ['lug fep', 'BBB']]
query = 'dax fep'
parts = []
for pair in study:
    parts.append(pair[0] + ' = ' + pair[1])
print(' | '.join(parts) + ' | ' + query)

items: Training details are modest: the Adam optimizer, 25 episodes per batch and 50 passes over the data, on a single graphics card. Dropout of 0.1 keeps the network from overfitting. The model is not large, so this is not about raw computing power.
In short, the recipe is: random grammars, many episodes, mixed targets, one plain transformer. That is the whole of MLC. The interesting finding is how far this simple recipe goes.

summary: MLC can be compared with people on the very same tasks. On the few-shot task its best run reached perfect exact-match accuracy, and its sampled answers matched human behaviour closely.
Sampled answers followed the rule 82.4 percent of the time, against 80.7 for people, and handled longer outputs 77.8 percent of the time against 72.5. Its types of mistakes also looked human.
A basic network scored zero, and a purely symbolic model with built-in biases needed much more hand-built structure to come close.

ELI5. Imagine a robot and a group of people sit the same test. We check not only how many they get right but also what kind of mistakes they make. If the robot slips in the same ways as people, it is probably thinking in a people-like way.

Now the real words. MLC reached 100 percent with its most likely answers and about 82.4 percent when sampling, against 80.7 for people. It also predicted which items were hard for them. Models are compared with log-likelihood, where numbers closer to zero are better.
Try it. Compute the log-likelihood of a few probabilities in the lab and see how a very unlikely answer drags the total way down.
If you remember one thing: MLC acts like people, a basic network gets zero.

Let us look at the scoreboard. First, a perfectly obedient network. Take the most systematic MLC run and let it always choose its most likely symbol. It reached 100 percent exact-match accuracy on the best responses. The rules were learned fully.

But people are not perfectly obedient. So the researchers let the network guess by chance, using its learned probabilities, as people do. In this mode MLC was systematic 82.4 percent of the time, close to people's 80.7. On longer outputs MLC got 77.8 percent against people's 72.5.

The figure compares them side by side. The blue bars are people, the purple bars are MLC. The two are close, and both are far above the red bar: a basic sequence-to-sequence network scored zero. (See Figure 8.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 8.1. People, MLC and a basic network on the few-shot task.

items: There is a deeper test of human-likeness than overall scores. When MLC made mistakes, they looked like human mistakes, such as one-to-one answers and iconic concatenation.
MLC also predicted which test items would be hard for people: the match between the model's item difficulty and human difficulty was a strong correlation of 0.788.

The paper scores models by log-likelihood: how likely the model thinks the actual human answers were. Higher is better. The joint MLC model scored about minus 349 on the few-shot task, a symbolic model with the same biases scored about minus 357, and a basic network scored minus 1,265, a huge gap.

On the open-ended task, where there are no examples, MLC answered like the most common person in 65 percent of its samples and also captured partial use of the habits. Its joint version beat the symbolic model with built-in biases by a wide margin there too.

# log-likelihood of three answers the model thought likely

probs = [0.5, 0.25, 0.8]
print('log-likelihood:', round(sum(math.log(p) for p in probs), 2))

items: The log-likelihood sum is easy to read: each answer's probability goes through a logarithm, so common answers contribute small negative numbers, and surprising answers contribute big negative numbers. A model that finds human answers more likely has a total closer to zero.
Memory trick: Less negative is more human. Log-likelihood closer to zero means the model finds human answers more likely.

summary: Besides the human tasks, the paper tests MLC on two machine-learning benchmarks: SCAN, which turns commands into actions, and COGS, which turns sentences into logical forms.
On the lexical generalization tests MLC slashed error rates. For example on SCAN add jump the error fell from 99.27 percent for a basic network to 0.22 percent.
But MLC still fails some tests, such as the SCAN length split and three COGS structural splits, where the error stays at 100 percent.

ELI5. Picture two exams. In the first, the teacher uses a word in a new way. In the second, the teacher gives a much longer or differently shaped question than any in practice. A student can ace the first and still struggle with the second.

Now the real words. SCAN turns commands like jump twice into actions, and COGS turns sentences into logical forms. MLC cut errors sharply on lexical tests, for example 99.27 percent down to 0.22 on SCAN add jump, but it still fails length and some structure splits.
Try it. Write the tiny SCAN translator in the lab and try run twice and jump thrice. Then compute an error rate for 22 wrong answers out of 10000.
If you remember one thing: great at new uses of known words, not yet at new lengths or shapes.

The benchmark SCAN is a classic test. A command like jump twice must become the actions JUMP JUMP. The words walk, run, look and jump are primitives, and words like twice and thrice are modifiers. It is the same compositional puzzle as our colour language.

In the add jump test, the network sees the word jump only on its own in training, never together with twice or thrice. It is tested on jump twice. A system with true compositional skill would succeed. A normal network fails: the paper reports a 99.27 percent error rate for the basic model.

MLC applies the same idea you saw before: practise on episodes in which the word meanings are shuffled. The input holds study examples and a query, and the network must work out the meaning of the shuffled words and combine them.
This time it was applied with standard transformer parts and modular reading of study examples.

The results are striking. On SCAN add jump the error fell from 99.27 to 0.22 percent. On around right it fell from 51.13 to 0.04 percent. On opposite right it fell from 100 to 0.06 percent. On COGS lexical generalization it fell from 6.08 to 0.87 percent. The figure shows the gaps.
(See Figure 9.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 9.1. Exact-match error rates on SCAN and COGS: basic network against MLC.

items: COGS is the second benchmark. It asks a network to turn English sentences into logical forms, meaning structured statements. The lexical generalization split tests whether a known word can be used in a new role.

# error rate: wrong answers divided by all answers, as a percent

items: MLC does not solve everything. It fails on the SCAN length split, where the commands in the test are much longer than any in training, and on three COGS structural splits where it must handle new sentence shapes. On these the error rate stays at 100 percent.

This is an important lesson about reading results honestly. A method can be superb at one kind of generalization, new uses of known words, and still be stuck on others, such as new lengths and new structures. Always ask which test a number came from.

summary: MLC shows that a plain neural network can acquire human-like systematic generalization from a smart training stream. It is a big step but not a finished story.
The authors list honest limits: entirely new structures, new symbols that were never seen, and full natural language are all outside what has been shown.
Future work may add this kind of specialised training to large language models and vision models, and may draw lessons from how children learn.

It cannot yet handle entirely new structures.

Children's word learning may offer further clues.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Benchmarks: SCAN and COGS:
• SCAN turns commands into actions.
• COGS turns sentences into logical forms.
• MLC cut lexical errors sharply.
• Add jump: 99.27 percent down to 0.22 percent.
• Length and some structure splits still fail.

ELI5. Every good science story ends with an honest list of things we do not know yet. A great answer is not the same as a finished answer, and a careful reader always asks what the experiment left out.

Now the real words. MLC works within the kinds of episodes it practised on, cannot invent new symbols without a pointer mechanism, and has not been shown on full natural language. The authors suggest adding specialised meta-training to large language and vision models.
Try it. Open the original paper and find Figure 1, Figure 2 and Table 1. Match each number you meet to what you have learned here and write down one thing the study did not do.
If you remember one thing: a new kind of practice can change what a network understands.

Good science always lists what it did not do. The authors are clear about the limits of MLC. First, it handles episodes like those it practised on. If you hand it an entirely new structure that was not in its training stream, it has no way to cope.

Second, it cannot invent new symbols. A pointer mechanism would be needed to let it copy a word it has never seen. Third, it has been tested on made-up tasks and benchmarks, not on full natural language or images.

The figure sums it up. On the left are the strengths: new combinations of known words, human-like habits learned from data, a plain transformer and strong results on lexical benchmarks. On the right are the things still to do. (See Figure 10.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 10.1. What MLC does and does not do yet.

items: How does MLC relate to other ideas? The authors say it resembles hierarchical Bayesian modelling, a statistical method that learns biases from many tasks, but uses neural networks for more expressive power.
It also sits between symbolic models, which are rule-based, and standard neural nets, which are pattern-based.

Where might it go next? The authors suggest adding specialised meta-training to large language models or vision models. They also draw a developmental parallel: children get better at learning new words as they gain experience, as if they too were meta-learning.

What can you take from the paper as a learner? A powerful idea: sometimes you do not need a new kind of machine. You need a new kind of practice. Changing what a network practises can change what it understands.

Now you can read the original. Open the paper and look at Figure 1, then Figure 2, then Table 1. Check how each number matches what you have learned here. Notice how the authors share their data and code so that others can repeat the work, which is how science earns trust.
